Let
\[
f(x)=\frac1{2-x}.
\]
We use a polynomial majorant of \(f\) of degree \(8\).

Define
\[
R(x)=x^4-\frac{16}{9}x^3+x^2-\frac{4}{21}x+\frac1{126}.
\]
This polynomial is chosen so that
\[
\int_0^1 (1-x)R(x)x^j\,dx=0\qquad j=0,1,2,3.
\]
Also
\[
R(2)=\frac{227}{42}.
\]

Now set
\[
P(x)=\frac{1+\dfrac{(1-x)R(x)^2}{R(2)^2}}{2-x}.
\]
The numerator vanishes at \(x=2\), so \(P\) is actually a polynomial of degree \(8\). For \(0\le x\le 1\),
\[
P(x)-\frac1{2-x}
=
\frac{(1-x)R(x)^2}{R(2)^2(2-x)}
\ge 0.
\]
Therefore, for any admissible law \(\mu\),
\[
\mathbb E_\mu[f(X)]\le \mathbb E_\mu[P(X)].
\]
Since \(P\) has degree \(8\), its expectation is fixed by the given moments and equals the uniform integral:
\[
\mathbb E_\mu[P(X)]=\int_0^1 P(x)\,dx.
\]
A direct division and integration gives
\[
\int_0^1 P(x)\,dx=\frac{14161}{20430}.
\]
Thus
\[
M\le \frac{14161}{20430}.
\]

It remains to see equality is attainable. The polynomial \(R\) is orthogonal to all polynomials of degree \(\le 3\) with respect to the positive weight \((1-x)\,dx\), so it has four simple roots in \((0,1)\). Let those roots be \(r_1,\dots,r_4\). The Gauss-Radau quadrature rule with nodes
\[
r_1,r_2,r_3,r_4,1
\]
is exact for every polynomial of degree at most \(8\). Hence there is a probability law supported on these five points whose first eight moments are
\[
\int_0^1 x^k\,dx=\frac1{k+1}.
\]
At each support point, \(P=f\), because \((1-x)R(x)^2=0\). Therefore equality is attained.

Finally, if equality holds for some law \(\mu\), then
\[
\int_0^1 (P-f)\,d\mu=0.
\]
Since \(P-f\ge 0\) and vanishes only at \(r_1,\dots,r_4,1\), the measure must be supported on exactly those nodes. The weights are then uniquely determined by the first five moments via a nonsingular Vandermonde system. So the maximizing law is unique.

\[
\boxed{M=\frac{14161}{20430}}
\]

The maximizing law is unique.
